sentences: Your next weekly rest period must start no later than the end of six 24-hour periods (6 × 24 hours) counted from the end of your previous weekly rest period.
There is one exception.
If you drive a single occasional passenger service, you may postpone the weekly rest for up to 12 consecutive 24-hour periods after a previous regular weekly rest.
This is allowed only under conditions, which include the following.
After using the exception, you must take either two regular weekly rests, or one regular and one reduced weekly rest of at least 24 hours (with the reduction made up later).
The vehicle must have the required recording equipment.
If you drive between 22:00 and 06:00, the vehicle must be multi-manned or your driving period must be cut to three hours.

sentences: On average you may not work more than 48 hours a week.
In a single week your working time can go up to 60 hours, but only if your average over four months stays at or below 48 hours a week.
Where a Member State uses the derogation in Article 8, the reference period for working out the 48-hour average can be longer, but never more than six months.
If you work for more than one employer, the hours for all of them are added together.
Your employer must ask you in writing how much time you worked for another employer, and you must give that information in writing.
Separately, your driving time alone must not exceed 56 hours in a week, and it must not push you over the weekly working-time maximum.

sentences: If you perform night work, your daily working time must not exceed 10 hours in each 24-hour period.
Night work means any work done during night time.
Night time is a period of at least 4 hours between 00.00 and 07.00, and your national law sets the exact period.
Compensation for night work is allowed under national law or collective agreements, but only if it does not endanger road safety.
Breaks, rest times and, in principle, periods of availability do not count as working time.

For those vehicles, enforcement officers may allow up to 15 minutes over each 4.5-hour block of driving, for example by deducting 1 minute per driving block between stops.

For the first hour, having the other driver(s) on board is optional.
For the rest of the period it is compulsory.

sentences: Periods of availability are periods, other than breaks and rest, when you do not have to stay at your workstation but must be available to answer calls to start or resume driving or to do other work.
They include time accompanying a vehicle carried by ferry or train, waiting at frontiers and waiting caused by traffic bans.

You must know these periods and their foreseeable duration in advance: before departure, just before the period starts, or under general conditions agreed by the social partners or set by national law.
For team drivers, time spent sitting next to the driver or on the couchette while the vehicle is moving also counts.
Periods of availability are excluded from working time.
However, national law or social-partner agreements may provide for them to be compensated or limited.
If you wait for loading or unloading without knowing in advance how long it will take, and you must stay at your workstation, that waiting counts as working time instead.

sentences: Under Directive 2002/15/EC you count as a self-employed driver only if ALL of these apply: your main occupation is carrying passengers or goods by road for hire or reward, under a Community licence or other professional authorisation; you are entitled to work for yourself; you are not tied to an employer by an employment contract or any other working hierarchical relationship; you are free to organise your own work; your income depends directly on the profits made; and you are free, alone or through a cooperation of self-employed drivers, to have commercial relations with several customers.
If you do not meet these criteria, you have the same obligations and rights as a mobile worker (employed driver) under the Directive.
The Directive applies to self-employed drivers from 23 March 2009.

Under Regulation 561/2006 a 'driver' is not only someone who actually drives, even for a short time.
It is also anyone carried in the vehicle as part of his duties to be available for driving if needed.
So a colleague riding along to relieve you counts as a driver.
While you drive, he may take his 45-minute break in the vehicle, as long as he is not helping you drive it.

sentences: Yes.
A regular daily rest (at least 11 hours) may be taken in two parts.
The first part must be an uninterrupted period of at least 3 hours and the second an uninterrupted period of at least 9 hours, so 12 hours in total.
A rest of at least 9 hours but less than 11 hours counts as a reduced daily rest.
You may take at most three reduced daily rests between any two weekly rests.
If you are on a ferry or train with a sleeper cabin, bunk or couchette, your regular daily rest may be interrupted at most twice, for no more than 1 hour in total.

Commission guidance note 6 (January 2017, older than the current consolidated Regulation) says that when the rest is split into two parts, the limit of two interruptions applies to the whole daily rest, not to each part.

sentences: A Member State may exempt these vehicles from the rules on driving times, breaks and rest (Articles 5 to 9 of Regulation 561/2006), as long as the aims of the Regulation are not undermined.
The Member State may add its own conditions.
The exemption can cover its own territory, or another Member State's territory if that State agrees.
All of the following must be met:
- The vehicle or combination has a maximum permissible mass of no more than 7,5 tonnes.
- It is used by a universal postal service provider to deliver items as part of the universal service.
- It is used only within 100 km of the undertaking's base.
- Driving is not the driver's main activity.
The Member State must tell the Commission about the exemption.
It may also exempt these vehicles from the tachograph Regulation (165/2014).

sentences: A regular weekly rest is at least 45 hours, so a 30-hour rest is a reduced weekly rest and you owe 15 hours.
Take those 15 hours in one block (not split up) before the end of the third week after the week in which you took the reduced rest.

It must be in suitable gender-friendly accommodation with adequate sleeping and sanitary facilities, and your employer pays for it.
Special case for international goods transport: if you took two reduced weekly rests in a row abroad, the compensation for both must be taken before your next weekly rest.

sentences: Driving: after 4.5 hours of driving you must take a break of at least 45 minutes without interruption, unless you take a rest period instead.
You can split this break into at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30 minutes, spread over the driving period.
If you drive an occasional passenger service, you may instead take two breaks of at least 15 minutes each.
Working: you must never work more than six hours in a row without a break.
If your working hours total between six and nine hours, you need a break of at least 30 minutes.
If they total more than nine hours, you need at least 45 minutes.
These working-time breaks apply without lowering the protection that the driving-time rules give you.

Article 8(8) requires these rests to be taken in suitable gender-friendly accommodation with adequate sleeping and sanitary facilities.
Article 8(8) states that any costs for accommodation outside the vehicle shall be covered by the employer.
Article 8(8) names exactly regular weekly rests and compensating weekly rests of more than 45 hours as the rests that may not be taken in a vehicle.
Article 8(8) does not mention reduced weekly rests, and Article 4(h) defines them as less than 45 hours and able to be shortened to a minimum of 24 consecutive hours.

sentences: Your company must plan your work so you can get back home within every period of four consecutive weeks.

"Home" here means either your place of residence or the employer's operational centre where you are normally based and where your weekly rest starts, in the Member State where the employer is established.
The trip back must let you spend at least one regular weekly rest, or a weekly rest of more than 45 hours taken as compensation for a reduced one.
Exception: if you have taken two reduced weekly rests in a row, the company must plan your work so you can get back before the compensating weekly rest of more than 45 hours begins.
The company must document how it meets this obligation and keep the records at its premises to show inspectors on request.

sentences.reason: Article 8(8a) requires undertakings to organise drivers' work so they can return within each period of four consecutive weeks.

Article 8(8a) names the two return points: the employer's operational centre where the driver is normally based and weekly rest begins, in the Member State of establishment, or the driver's place of residence; the Member State condition attaches to the operational centre, but the sentence's grouping is a reasonable paraphrase.
Article 8(8a) states the return is in order to spend at least one regular weekly rest or a weekly rest of more than 45 hours taken in compensation for a reduced one.
The second paragraph of Article 8(8a) requires return before the start of the compensating rest of more than 45 hours where two consecutive reduced weekly rests were taken.
The last paragraph of Article 8(8a) requires the undertaking to document compliance and keep the documentation at its premises for control authorities on request.

sentences: Not yet, but they will from 1 July 2026.
Today the EU driving time rules cover goods vehicles over 3,5 tonnes, so a 3-tonne van is outside them.
From 1 July 2026 the rules also cover goods vehicles over 2,5 tonnes (including any trailer) used in international transport or cabotage, and your cross-border deliveries will be included.
Exceptions still apply to vans over 2,5 t and up to 3,5 t when the transport is not for hire or reward but on the own account of the company or driver, and driving is not the driver's main activity.
Vehicles up to 7,5 t are also exempt for non-commercial carriage of goods.

They are also exempt when carrying the driver's own work materials or equipment, or delivering craft-produced goods, within 100 km of base, not for hire or reward, and where driving is not the driver's main activity.
Separately, a Commission note says that outside the EU scope a country may apply its own national rules modelled on the EU rules.
That note dates from 1993, before the 2020 Mobility Package changed the rules.

sentences.reason: The claim that 3-tonne cross-border goods vans are not covered now but will be from 1 July 2026 follows from Article 2(1)(a) (over 3,5 t) and Article 2(1)(aa) (from 1 July 2026, international goods transport over 2,5 t).
Article 2(1)(a) applies the Regulation to goods vehicles over 3,5 tonnes, so a 3-tonne van falls outside that threshold.
Article 2(1)(aa) extends coverage from 1 July 2026 to goods vehicles over 2,5 tonnes, including any trailer, in international transport or cabotage operations.
Article 3(ha) exempts goods vehicles over 2,5 t and up to 3,5 t when the transport is on own account, not for hire or reward, and driving is not the driver's main activity.
Article 3(h) exempts vehicles up to 7,5 tonnes used for the non-commercial carriage of goods.

Article 3(aa) exempts vehicles up to 7,5 t carrying the driver's work materials or equipment, or delivering craft-produced goods, within 100 km of base, where driving is not the main activity and the transport is not for hire or reward.
Clarification note 1 states that Member States are free to legislate outside the Regulation's scope and may adopt national rules inspired by or identical to the EU rules.
The note's place attribute states it was published in February 1993, before the 2020 Mobility Package changed the rules.

sentences: Yes.
Since 2 February 2022, when you cross into another Member State you must enter that country's symbol in the digital tachograph at the start of your first stop there.
That stop must be made at the nearest possible stopping place at or after the border.
If you cross on a ferry or train, enter the symbol at the port or station of arrival.
You must also still enter the countries where your daily working period started and finished.
You do not have to enter those start and finish countries if your tachograph records location automatically under Article 8.
Note that this exemption, as written, refers only to the start and finish countries, not to the border-crossing entry.
Smart tachographs in vehicles first registered more than two years after the relevant detailed provisions entered into force also record each Member State border crossing automatically.

sentences.reason: The affirmative answer is borne out by Article 34(7), which requires the driver to enter the country symbol after crossing a Member State border.
Article 34(7) second subparagraph states that from 2 February 2022 the driver enters the symbol of the country entered at the beginning of the first stop there.
Article 34(7) states that the first stop shall be made at the nearest possible stopping place at or after the border.
Article 34(7) states that for crossings on a ferry or train the symbol is entered at the port or station of arrival.
Article 34(7) first subparagraph requires entering the symbols of the countries where the daily working period started and finished.
Article 34(7) last subparagraph removes the need to enter the first-subparagraph information when the tachograph records location automatically under Article 8.

The exemption in Article 34(7) refers only to 'the information referred to in the first subparagraph', which is the start and finish countries, not the border-crossing entry in the second subparagraph.

Article 8(1) ties automatic border-crossing recording to vehicles first registered more than two years after the detailed provisions in the second paragraph of Article 11 entered into force, but its text applies this to vehicles 'registered in a Member State for the first time', which the sentence restates closely enough.
